B1

Here is the dashboard running live. It is one HTML file in the repository, so it opens on any laptop without a server, and it is also on GitHub Pages. I am replaying the test fortnight. Right now it is 2:15 in the afternoon on Monday the 21st of September, day 15.
B2

On the left is the clinic's patient list: fourteen held-out test patients, ranked by the risk of a spike above 180 in the next two hours. Each row shows the current glucose, a trend arrow and the risk. 'High now' means the patient is already above 180.
B3
The top patient is PT-185: a 44-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes, HbA1c 7.3 percent, on metformin, with hypertension and obesity. This comes from her synthetic health record.
B4

The alert card says 95 percent risk of going above 180 and 38 percent risk of going above 250, with a forecast high of about 307 within the hour. Her glucose right now is only 141, so the number alone looks fine. The reasons: the twin's predicted peak, the time of day, and how variable her glucose has been in the last three hours. And the suggested nudge: a 15-minute walk now would take about 14 off her peak.
B5

This chart shows why. In black, her last twelve hours of CGM. The orange triangle is the lunch she logged 14 minutes ago: two katori of rice with dal and curd, about 132 grams of carbohydrate. The teal line is Prahari's forecast with its 80 percent band, and the dashed orange line is the twin on its own. In grey, because this is a replay, you can see what actually happened: she peaked at about 339, higher than forecast. It was a short night and a stressful working day for her, and the model cannot see stress directly. That is a real limit, and the band shows the uncertainty.
B6

Now the what-if panel. This runs her calibrated twin inside the browser. With no walk, the twin predicts a peak of 297 and two hours above 180. A 15-minute walk brings the peak to 283 and saves fifteen minutes above 180. A 30-minute walk brings it to 269.
B7
She slept only 4.9 hours last night. If she had slept a full seven and a half hours, the same walk would bring the peak to 275, because sleep loss lowers insulin sensitivity.
B8

Here is her twin. Her record suggested an insulin sensitivity of 2.9; after two weeks of CGM, the twin estimates 5.4, so she responds to insulin better than her record implied. But her fasting level is higher than expected, 149 against 130. That tells a doctor where to look first: her mornings and her large meals.
B9

Below are the wearables for the last 24 hours: steps, heart rate, heart-rate variability and last night's sleep stages. You can see the short night. On the right, her last seven days as an ambulatory glucose profile: 77 percent time in range, with clear peaks after lunch and dinner.
Let me press play and move time forward. Every step is 15 minutes, and the list re-ranks itself as patients eat, walk and sleep. I will stop at 8 pm, before dinner.

It is 8 pm and dinner is coming. The doctor can plan it with her. Two katori of rice would take her to a predicted 268. Switching to chapati, dal and sabzi brings that to 224, and with a 15-minute walk, 215. Cut the portion to 70 percent as well and the peak is 195, and time above 180 falls from two hours to about 70 minutes. This is the kind of concrete, personal advice that a single HbA1c number cannot give.

Now another patient: PT-046, a 58-year-old man with prediabetes. His risk is 56 percent, just over the alert threshold, with a forecast high of 193 in two hours. The reasons say his usual dinner time is approaching. Prahari learned his routine in the first week, so it can warn before a meal, not only after it.
The alerts filter shows only the patients above the alert threshold right now. At 8 pm on this Monday, that is four of the fourteen.

The model evidence tab is for the jury and for clinicians who want to check the numbers. First, forecast error on the 41 held-out patients: Prahari is the best at every horizon, 17.2 at 30 minutes and 24.2 at two hours. Next, the alerts: about three in four spikes above 180 are flagged with a median 85-minute warning. Severe spikes above 250 remain hard. Then the SHAP chart, what drives an alert overall; teal bars come from the twin. Then the identifiability check: the twin's estimates against the hidden truth, a rank correlation of 0.81 for insulin sensitivity, against 0.37 from the record alone. And at the bottom, the realism checks against published studies.

Finally, the How it works tab summarises the five layers and the limits, so anyone opening the page understands what they are looking at. That is the live demo. Let me close with how this would work in India.
